# vec_arena - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vec-arena/

A simple object arena.

`Arena<T>` is basically just a `Vec<Option<T>>`, which allows you to:

- Insert an object (reuse an existing `None`
- Remove object at a specified index.
- Access object at a specified index.

Some data structures built using `Arena<T>`:

# vec-arena 1.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/vec-arena/latest

# vec-arena (deprecated)

**This crate is now deprecated in favor of  slab.**

#### What is this?

A simple object arena.

You want to build a doubly linked list? Or maybe a bidirectional tree? Perhaps an even more complicated object graph?

Managing ownership and lifetimes might be tough then. Your options boil down to:

- Use unsafe code to escape Rust's ownership rules.
- Wrap every object in `Rc<RefCell<T>>`.
- Use `Vec<T>`to store objects, then access them using indices.

If the last option seems most appealing to you, perhaps `Arena<T>` is for you.
It will provide a more convenient API than a plain `Vec<T>`.

#### Examples

Some data structures built using `Arena<T>`:

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# gvm-auth-cli 0.2.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/gvm-auth-cli/0.2.3

# GVM Authentication Library (gvm-auth-lib)

The GVM Authentication Library is a Rust library for common authentication functionality used within the Greenbone Vulnerability Manager such as the generation of JSON Web Tokens and communicating with authentication APIs like OAuth and OpenID Connect.

The library is mostly implemented in Rust but a wrapper for use in C is also included. The components are organized as a Rust workspace consisting of multiple crates.

## Main Rust library (gvm-auth)

The `gvm-auth` crate is the main library for use in Rust.

It can be built with the standard Cargo command

```
cargo build -p gvm-auth
```
## C wrapper library (gvm-auth-c)

The `gvm-auth-c` crate is a wrapper of the library for use in C.

It can be built with the standard Cargo command

```
cargo build -p gvm-auth-c
```
In case of build-time errors, it can be useful to exclude the C header file generation as cargo and rustc often give more helpful error messages than cbindgen.

To do this, you can disable the default features when building the crate:

```
cargo build -p gvm-auth-c --no-default-features
```
### Preparing the installation and tests

To automatically install the C library or build the Cgreen tests, first create a build directory and initialize the CMake project inside with the same installation prefix as gvm-libs and other GVM modules like gvmd.

```
mkdir build
cd build
cmake -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=~/my-gvm-prefix ..
```
### Installation

If the prefix is set up correctly, you should be able to install the library, header file and pkgconfig file with the standard make target:

```
make install
```
It can then be added as a dependency to other CMake projects as
`libgvm_auth`:

```
pkg_check_modules(LIBGVM_AUTH REQUIRED libgvm_auth>=0.1.0)
```
### Cgreen tests

Inside the build directory you can build the tests with the make target `tests`
and then run them with the `test` target:

```
make tests
make test
```
## CLI tools (gvm-auth-cli)

The `gvm-auth-cli` crate is a command line tool for testing various functions
of the GVM authentication libary `gvm-auth-lib`.

It can be built with the standard Cargo command

```
cargo build -p gvm-auth-cli
```

# calib_targets - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets/0.10.0/calib_targets/

## Expand description

High-level facade crate for the `calib-targets-*` workspace.

This crate provides:

- stable, convenient re-exports of the underlying detector crates
- (feature-gated) end-to-end helpers that run a ChESS corner detector
(`chess-corners`) and then run a target detector on an image or raw buffer.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets::detect;
use calib_targets::chessboard::DetectorParams;
use image::ImageReader;
let img = ImageReader::open("board.png")?.decode()?.to_luma8();
let params = DetectorParams::default();
let result = detect::detect_chessboard(&img, &detect::default_chess_config(), ¶ms);
println!("detected: {}", result.is_some());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#python-bindings)Python bindings

Python bindings live in `crates/calib-targets-py` and expose the
`calib_targets` module. See `crates/calib-targets-py/README.md` in the
repository for setup, the `detect_*` APIs, and printable-target generation.
Config inputs accept typed Python classes; `detect_charuco` requires
`params` with `params.board`. For marker boards, `target_position` is
populated only when `params.layout.cell_size` is provided and alignment
succeeds.

[§](https://docs.rs#api-map)API map

- `calib_targets::core`: core types (corners, grids, homographies, images).
- `calib_targets::chessboard`: chessboard detection from ChESS corners.
- `calib_targets::aruco`: ArUco/AprilTag dictionaries and marker decoding.
- `calib_targets::charuco`: ChArUco board alignment and IDs.
- `calib_targets::puzzleboard`: PuzzleBoard edge-code decoding and IDs.
- `calib_targets::marker`: checkerboard + circle marker boards.
- `calib_targets::printable`: printable target generation and JSON/SVG/PNG output.
- `calib_targets::detect`(feature- `image`): end-to-end helpers from- `image::GrayImage`.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

Benchmarks are coming. The goal is to be the fastest detector in this class while maintaining high sensitivity and accuracy.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [calib_targets_aruco](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-aruco/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_aruco/index.html)as aruco;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_charuco](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-charuco/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_charuco/index.html)as charuco;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_chessboard](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-chessboard/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_chessboard/index.html)as chessboard;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_core](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_core/index.html)as core;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_marker](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-marker/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_marker/index.html)as marker;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_print](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-print/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_print/index.html)as printable;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_puzzleboard](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-puzzleboard/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_puzzleboard/index.html)as puzzleboard;

# yatrosci_bio_systems - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-bio-systems/0.1.0/yatrosci_bio_systems/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-systems-biology-advanced)SciRS Systems Biology (Advanced)

Formal modeling of biological networks and systems. No simplified equations.

This crate provides:

- Mass-action kinetics (law of mass action, reaction order)
- Metabolic Control Analysis (MCA) (Elasticities, Control coefficients)
- Stoichiometric Modeling (Flux Balance Analysis foundations)
- Gene Regulatory Networks (Hill kinetics, cooperativity, Hill plot)

[§](https://docs.rs#references)References

- Hill, A. V. (1910). The possible effects of the aggregation of the
molecules of haemoglobin on its dissociation curves.
*J. Physiol.*40, iv–vii.
- Guldberg, C. M., & Waage, P. (1864). Studies concerning affinity.
*Forhandlinger: Videnskabs-Selskabet i Christiania*. (Law of mass action.)
- Kacser, H., & Burns, J. A. (1973). The control of flux.
*Symp. Soc. Exp. Biol.*27, 65–104. (Metabolic Control Analysis; flux-control summation theorem.)
- Palsson, B. Ø. (2015). *Systems Biology: Constraint-based Reconstruction and Analysis*. Cambridge University Press. DOI:[10.1017/CBO9781139854610](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139854610)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [control](https://docs.rs/control/index.html)
- Sensitivity and Control
- [mass_](https://docs.rs/mass_action/index.html)- action
- Mass-action kinetics (law of mass action).
- [metabolism](https://docs.rs/metabolism/index.html)
- Stoichiometric and Flux Analysis
- [regulation](https://docs.rs/regulation/index.html)
- Regulatory Kinetics

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- Error type for systems biology

# calib_targets_print - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-print/0.10.0/calib_targets_print/

## Expand description

Printable calibration target generation.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# calib_targets_puzzleboard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-puzzleboard/0.10.0/calib_targets_puzzleboard/

## Expand description

PuzzleBoard calibration target detector.

The *PuzzleBoard* is a self-identifying chessboard target introduced by
Stelldinger (2024, [arXiv:2409.20127](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.20127)):
a standard checkerboard with a small binary dot placed at the midpoint of
every interior edge. The dot pattern is designed so that any locally
observed fragment of the board (≥ 4 × 4 squares) uniquely identifies its
absolute position on a master 501 × 501 pattern — giving every detected
chessboard corner an absolute `(I, J)` label, with graceful degradation
under occlusion, perspective distortion, and low pixel-per-edge ratios.

Encoding is the superposition of two cyclic binary sub-perfect maps:

- **A**: shape- `(3, 167)`with window- `(3, 3)₂`— one bit per horizontal edge
- **B**: shape- `(167, 3)`with window- `(3, 3)₂`— one bit per vertical edge

The maps are generated once (see `tools/generate_code_maps.rs`) and shipped
as embedded bytes (`src/data/map_a.bin` / `map_b.bin`). All runtime lookups
go through [ code_maps](https://docs.rs/code_maps/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_puzzleboard::{
    PuzzleBoardDetector, PuzzleBoardParams, PuzzleBoardSpec,
};
let spec = PuzzleBoardSpec::new(12, 12, 1.0)?;
let params = PuzzleBoardParams::for_board(&spec);
let detector = PuzzleBoardDetector::new(params)?;
// Feed a real greyscale image and raw ChESS corners to `detector.detect(…)`.
// See `examples/detect_puzzleboard.rs` for a working end-to-end example.
```

- `pub use code_maps::`- [EDGE_MAP_A_ROWS](https://docs.rs/code_maps/constant.EDGE_MAP_A_ROWS.html);
- `pub use code_maps::`- [EDGE_MAP_B_COLS](https://docs.rs/code_maps/constant.EDGE_MAP_B_COLS.html);
- `pub use code_maps::`- [EDGE_MAP_B_ROWS](https://docs.rs/code_maps/constant.EDGE_MAP_B_ROWS.html);

- `pub use diagnostics::`- [PuzzleBoardDiagnostics](https://docs.rs/diagnostics/struct.PuzzleBoardDiagnostics.html);

# calib_targets_marker - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-marker/0.10.0/calib_targets_marker/

## Expand description

Checkerboard marker target detector (checkerboard + 3 circles in the middle).

Pipeline overview:

- Detect a chessboard grid from ChESS corners (partial boards are allowed).
- Score circular markers per-cell in image space.
- Match circle candidates to the known layout and estimate the grid offset.
- Return typed marker-board corners with optional board alignment.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_chessboard::ChessCorner;
use calib_targets_core::GrayImageView;
use calib_targets_marker::{
    CellCoords, CirclePolarity, MarkerBoardDetector, MarkerBoardSpec, MarkerBoardParams,
    MarkerCircleSpec,
};
let layout = MarkerBoardSpec::new(
    6,
    8,
    [
        MarkerCircleSpec::new(CellCoords { i: 2, j: 2 }, CirclePolarity::White),
        MarkerCircleSpec::new(CellCoords { i: 3, j: 2 }, CirclePolarity::Black),
        MarkerCircleSpec::new(CellCoords { i: 2, j: 3 }, CirclePolarity::White),
    ],
)
.with_cell_size(1.0);
let params = MarkerBoardParams::new(layout);
let detector = MarkerBoardDetector::new(params).expect("valid chessboard config");
let pixels = vec![0u8; 32 * 32];
let view = GrayImageView {
    width: 32,
    height: 32,
    data: &pixels,
};
let corners: Vec<ChessCorner> = Vec::new();
let _ = detector.detect_from_image_and_corners(&view, &corners);
```

# calib_targets_aruco - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-aruco/0.10.0/calib_targets_aruco/

## Expand description

ArUco/AprilTag marker dictionaries and decoding utilities.

This crate focuses on:

- embedded built-in dictionaries (compiled into the binary),
- matching observed marker codes against those dictionaries,
- decoding markers either from rectified grids or from per-cell image quads.

It does **not** perform quad detection. Instead, it expects a grid model
(for example from `calib-targets-chessboard`) or explicit cell corners.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_aruco::{
    builtins, scan_decode_markers, GrayImageView, Matcher, ScanDecodeConfig,
};
let dict = builtins::builtin_dictionary("DICT_4X4_50").expect("dict");
let matcher = Matcher::new(dict, 1);
let pixels = vec![0u8; 16 * 16];
let view = GrayImageView {
    width: 16,
    height: 16,
    data: &pixels,
};
let scan_cfg = ScanDecodeConfig::default();
let markers = scan_decode_markers(&view, 4, 4, 4.0, &scan_cfg, &matcher);
println!("markers: {}", markers.len());
```

# calib_targets_chessboard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-chessboard/0.10.0/calib_targets_chessboard/

## Expand description

Invariant-first chessboard detector.

Takes a slice of [ChESS](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/research/rainbow/projects/chess/)
X-junction corners and returns an integer-labelled chessboard grid. The
crate’s only output contract is: *every labelled corner has been proven
to sit at a real grid intersection.* Missing corners are acceptable;
wrong corners are not.

**High detection rate on our private regression set with zero wrong
 (i, j) labels** (non-negligible lens distortion and motion blur).

Algorithm reference: see `book/src/chessboard.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline)Pipeline

The detector builds its `(i, j)` labelling with the **topological** grid
finder in [ projective_grid](https://docs.rs/projective-grid/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/projective_grid/index.html) (a Delaunay triangulation + an axis-driven
cell test), then runs a chessboard-specific recovery + precision pass over
the labelled components:

| Stage | Name | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `prefilter` | Drop corners failing strength / fit-quality / axes-validity gates. |
| 2 | `cluster_axes` | Recover the two global grid-direction centres `{Θ₀, Θ₁}`via histogram + 2-means; label each corner as canonical or swapped. |
| 3 | `topological_grid` | Delaunay + axis-driven cell test → connected labelled `(i, j)`components ().`projective_grid::detect_grid_all` |
| 4 | `recover_components` | Per-component recall boosters (interior gap fill + line extrapolation with a directional edge scale) + shared component merge. |
| 5 | `final_geometry_check` | Mandatory precision gate: line collinearity + local-H residual + direct wrong-label check + largest cardinal component. Can only drop corners; never adds. |
| 6 | `output` | Labelled grid → canonicalised, non-negative-rebased .`ChessboardDetection` |

Each stage is its own module or function; see the submodules.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_chessboard::{ChessCorner, Detector, DetectorParams};
use calib_targets_core::AxisEstimate;
use nalgebra::Point2;
// A synthetic 7×7 chessboard corner cloud at 20 px pitch. Adjacent
// corners carry opposite axis-slot orderings (the parity invariant).
let mut corners: Vec<ChessCorner> = Vec::new();
for j in 0..7 {
    for i in 0..7 {
        let swapped = (i + j) % 2 == 1;
        let (a0, a1) = if swapped {
            (std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_2, 0.0)
        } else {
            (0.0, std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_2)
        };
        corners.push(ChessCorner {
            position: Point2::new(i as f32 * 20.0 + 50.0, j as f32 * 20.0 + 50.0),
            axes: [
                AxisEstimate { angle: a0, sigma: 0.01 },
                AxisEstimate { angle: a1, sigma: 0.01 },
            ],
            contrast: 10.0,
            fit_rms: 1.0,
            // Above the default `min_corner_strength` floor (33.0).
            strength: 100.0,
        });
    }
}
let det = Detector::new(DetectorParams::default()).expect("default params are valid");
let detection = det.detect(&corners).expect("clean 7×7 grid detects");
assert_eq!(detection.corners.len(), 49);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rectification-helpers)Rectification helpers

Two rectifiers are exposed: [ rectify_from_chessboard_result](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_from_chessboard_result.html)
(

[) and](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedBoardView.html)

`RectifiedBoardView`[(](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_mesh_from_grid.html)

`rectify_mesh_from_grid`[). The former takes a](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedMeshView.html)

`RectifiedMeshView`[directly; the latter is pattern-agnostic and takes a](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessboardDetection.html)

`ChessboardDetection``&[LabeledCorner]` plus an inlier index list. Both produce a
rectified view and can be used with any consistent `(i, j)`
labelling.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Advanced, **unstable**per-stage tuning knobs for the chessboard detector.

# calib_targets_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-core/0.10.0/calib_targets_core/

## Expand description

Core types and utilities for calibration target detection.

This crate is intentionally small and purely geometric. It does *not*
depend on any concrete corner detector implementation or image type, but it
owns the shared detector configuration contracts used across the workspace.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_core::{LabeledCorner, TargetDetection, TargetKind};
use nalgebra::Point2;
let corner = LabeledCorner::new(Point2::new(12.0, 8.0), 0.9);
let detection = TargetDetection::new(TargetKind::Chessboard, vec![corner]);
println!("{}", detection.corners.len());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#includes)Includes

- Homography estimation and warping helpers.
- Lightweight grayscale image views and sampling.
- Grid alignment and target detection types.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Shared JSON IO helpers for config and report types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Axis](https://docs.rs/struct.AxisEstimate.html)- Estimate
- Local estimate of one undirected grid axis at a detected corner.
- [Coord](https://docs.rs/struct.Coord.html)
- The canonical integer grid-coordinate type `(u, v)`—`u`is the grid’s first axis (right),`v`the second (down). Re-exported from`projective_grid`
- [Detector](https://docs.rs/struct.DetectorConfig.html)- Config
- High-level detection configuration.
- [Gray](https://docs.rs/struct.GrayImage.html)- Image
- Owned 8-bit grayscale image.
- [Gray](https://docs.rs/struct.GrayImageView.html)- Image - View
- Borrowed view over an 8-bit grayscale image.
- [Grid](https://docs.rs/struct.GridAlignment.html)- Alignment
- A grid alignment: `dst = transform(src) + translation`.
- [Grid](https://docs.rs/struct.GridTransform.html)- Transform
- Integer 2D grid transform (a 2×2 matrix) for aligning detected grids to a board model.
- [Homography](https://docs.rs/struct.Homography.html)
- A 3×3 projective homography matrix.
- [Homography](https://docs.rs/struct.HomographyQuality.html)- Quality
- Numerical quality of a homography matrix.
- [Labeled](https://docs.rs/struct.LabeledCorner.html)- Corner
- A corner that is part of a detected target, with optional ID info.
- [Rectified](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedView.html)- View
- A rectified (fronto-parallel) view of a detected board, plus the mapping back to the original image.
- [Target](https://docs.rs/struct.TargetDetection.html)- Detection
- One detected target (board instance) in an image.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Orientation](https://docs.rs/enum.OrientationMethod.html)- Method
- Method used to fit the two grid axes at a detected corner.
- [Rect](https://docs.rs/enum.RectToImgMapper.html)- ToImg - Mapper
- Mapping from rectified-image coordinates back to original-image coordinates.
- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.TargetKind.html)- Kind
- The kind of target that a detection corresponds to.

- The 8 dihedral transforms `D4`on the integer grid.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [axis_](https://docs.rs/fn.axis_estimate_from_next.html)- estimate_ - from_ - next
- Project a `NextLocalAxis`
- [axis_](https://docs.rs/fn.axis_estimate_to_next.html)- estimate_ - to_ - next

- [cell_](https://docs.rs/fn.cell_rect_corners_at.html)- rect_ - corners_ - at
- The four corners of a unit grid cell at `gc`, in canonical rectified space, in clockwise**TL, TR, BR, BL**order (the workspace-wide quad/homography order).
- [complete_](https://docs.rs/fn.complete_cell_corners.html)- cell_ - corners
- The four image corners of the unit cell whose top-left intersection is grid
`(u, v)`, in**TL, TR, BR, BL**order (clockwise — the canonical quad order used for every homography fit in the workspace). Returns`None`if any of the cell’s four grid intersections is absent from the map.
- [corner_](https://docs.rs/fn.corner_map_bounds.html)- map_ - bounds
- Inclusive grid-coordinate bounds `(min_u, min_v, max_u, max_v)`over a corner map’s keys, or`None`when the map is empty.
- [estimate_](https://docs.rs/fn.estimate_homography_rect_to_img.html)- homography_ - rect_ - to_ - img
- Estimate H such that `p_dst ~ H * p_src`from N >= 4 point correspondences.
- [estimate_](https://docs.rs/fn.estimate_homography_with_quality.html)- homography_ - with_ - quality
- Estimate H such that `p_dst ~ H * p_src`from N >= 4 point correspondences, returning the matrix together with its`HomographyQuality`
- [grid_](https://docs.rs/fn.grid_transform_from_next.html)- transform_ - from_ - next
- Project a `NextGridTransform`
- [grid_](https://docs.rs/fn.grid_transform_to_next.html)- transform_ - to_ - next
- Convert the legacy `GridTransform`into a tagged square-lattice transform for`projective_grid`
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_from_4pt.html)- from_ - 4pt
- Compute H from exactly 4 point correspondences: `dst ~ H * src`.
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_from_4pt_with_quality.html)- from_ - 4pt_ - with_ - quality
- 4-point variant of `estimate_homography_with_quality`
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_from_next.html)- from_ - next
- Project a `Projective2<f32>``Homography`
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_to_next.html)- to_ - next
- Convert `Homography`
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_tracing.html)- tracing
- Install a global `tracing`subscriber (available with the`tracing`feature).
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_with_level.html)- with_ - level
- Install the simple logger with the provided level filter.
- [log_](https://docs.rs/fn.log_sigmoid.html)- sigmoid
- Numerically stable `log(sigmoid(x))`.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_bilinear.html)- bilinear
- Bilinearly sample a grayscale image at sub-pixel `(x, y)`.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_bilinear_fast.html)- bilinear_ - fast
- Bilinearly sample a grayscale image, skipping bounds checks on the hot path.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_bilinear_u8.html)- bilinear_ - u8
- Bilinearly sample a grayscale image and round the result to `u8`.
- [square_](https://docs.rs/fn.square_predict_grid_position.html)- predict_ - grid_ - position
- Predict a square-grid corner position from complete cardinal neighbor pairs.
- [warp_](https://docs.rs/fn.warp_perspective_gray.html)- perspective_ - gray
- Warp into a rectified image: for each destination pixel center, map to
source image coordinates via `H_img_from_rect`and bilinear-sample.

# projective_grid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/projective-grid/0.10.0/projective_grid/

## Expand description

Target-agnostic projective grid recovery primitives.

This crate is intentionally small at the public boundary. It models two lattice families, two tasks, and explicit evidence shapes. Target-specific identifiers and detector classes belong in caller crates and should be converted into generic point features or coordinate hypotheses before entering this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-references)Design references

The crate is organised around three orthogonal axes — lattice family,
recovery strategy, and input-feature kind. The architecture and the
orientation-as-an-optional-cue model are documented under `docs/` in the
crate source tree:

- `docs/DESIGN.md`— the three design axes, the shared pipeline back-half, and how the lattice family extends to hex.
- `docs/ORIENTATION.md`— where each strategy consumes per-corner orientation and how each can run orientation-free (the dot-grid path).

The per-strategy stage maps live in `docs/algorithms/topological-grid-detection.md`
(repo root) and `calib-targets-chessboard/docs/PIPELINE.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#two-public-tiers)Two public tiers

The crate ships an intentional two-tier public API. Both tiers are supported; they differ in audience and in how fast the surface is allowed to move.

[§](https://docs.rs#stable-tier--the-facade-ordinary-users)Stable tier — the facade (ordinary users)

The items re-exported at the crate root are the supported surface for an
ordinary caller who wants to *detect a grid* and read the labels back:

- the entry points `detect_grid``detect_grid_all``check_consistency`
- the request types `Evidence``DetectionParams``DetectionRequest``ConsistencyParams``ConsistencyRequest`
- the result types `GridSolution``LabelledGrid``DetectionReport`
- the lattice model `Lattice``LatticeKind``Coord``PointFeature``OrientedFeature``LocalAxis`
- the orientation-synthesis helpers (`synthesize_oriented2``cluster_axes``AxisClusterCenters``AxisAssignment`

This tier carries normal semver guarantees: breaking changes here go through the usual deprecation cycle.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-tier--the-composition-api-build-your-own-detector)Advanced tier — the composition API (build your own detector)

[ shared](https://docs.rs/shared/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/topological/index.html)

`topological`[,](https://docs.rs/lattice/index.html)

`lattice`[, and](https://docs.rs/orient/index.html)

`orient`[expose the assembly engine the facade is built from, as a deliberate](https://docs.rs/cluster/index.html)

`cluster`**composition API**. It exists so a consumer with its own per-pattern invariants — the in-workspace chessboard detector is the reference example, but the contract is written for external consumers too — can drive the same grid-growth and recovery machinery under its own policy instead of going through the one-size-fits-all facade. This is intended product, not a private engine that merely happens to be

`pub`.The composition contract — what a consumer supplies and what the engine guarantees in return:

- **You supply a**This is the seam between the geometry-only growth machinery and your pattern’s rules. The policy answers four questions per candidate —- `shared::grow::SquareAttachPolicy`- `is_eligible`,- `required_label_at`,- `accept_candidate`,- `edge_ok`— letting you veto an attachment that is geometrically plausible but illegal for your pattern (e.g. a chessboard’s alternating-colour parity, or a per-corner blacklist). The engine never relabels behind your back: every attachment it proposes has already passed your policy.
- **You drive the growth / recovery engine.**The geometry-only primitives live under- `shared`- `shared::grow`- `shared::fill`- `shared::extension`- `shared::grow_extend`- `shared::recovery_schedule`- `RecoverySchedule`- `RecoveryParams`
- **You compose the shared back-half.**After your front-half has built integer-labelled components, the lattice-parameterised back-half reunites them with local geometry only (- `shared::merge`- `shared::validate`- `Lattice`
- **The guarantees.**Every stage is- *drop-only*with respect to labels: a corner whose geometry does not cohere is removed, never relabelled. The precision contract of the facade —- **zero wrong**, misses acceptable — therefore holds for a consumer that composes the engine under its own policy, because the policy gates and the validate/drop filters run on every attachment exactly as they do on the facade path. Returned components are rebased so the labelled bounding-box minimum is- `(i, j)`labels- `(0, 0)`; quad / homography corner order is TL, TR, BR, BL.

**Stability of the advanced tier.** This surface is *advanced, and may
evolve*: its shape tracks the engine’s internal structure, so an item may
change between minor releases when the engine is refactored. That is a
deliberate product choice — the tier trades a slower-moving contract for
direct access to the engine — not a disclaimer that it is really private.
If you only need to detect a grid, depend on the facade; reach for the
composition tier when you are building a *new kind of detector* on top of
the engine. Engine items with no external consumer stay `pub(crate)`, so
the advanced surface is kept no wider than what a consumer actually
composes.

[§](https://docs.rs#core-vs-extended-surface)Core vs. extended surface

Orthogonal to the stable/advanced split is a second distinction worth making explicit, because the two halves are exercised very differently in practice:

- **Core path (exercised in production).**The square lattice (- `LatticeKind::Square`- `Evidence::Oriented2`
- **Extended path (library-only breadth).**The hexagonal lattice (- `Hex`- `topological`- `D6_TRANSFORMS`- `orient`- `shared::recovery_schedule`- `Evidence::Positions`- `Evidence::Oriented1`- `docs/DESIGN.md`for the full core-vs-extended map.

# lash_provider_auth - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lash-provider-auth/0.1.0-alpha.82/lash_provider_auth/

## Expand description

Shared OAuth primitives used by provider crates that implement OAuth-based auth (Codex, Google). API-key backends bypass this module.

Provider-specific endpoints, device-code flows, PKCE helpers, and
refresh logic live in each provider crate under `oauth.rs`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_query_param.html)- query_ - param
- Extract the value of a given query parameter from a URL or raw
query-string. Returns `None`if the key is absent.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_pkce.html)- pkce
- Generate a PKCE code verifier and challenge pair. PKCE verifier is 32 bytes of OS entropy (via two UUID v4s) base64url-encoded; the challenge is its SHA-256 base64url-encoded.
- [now_](https://docs.rs/fn.now_secs.html)- secs
- [percent_](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_decode.html)- decode
- Percent-decode a query-string value (handles `+`→ space).
- [url_](https://docs.rs/fn.url_form_encode.html)- form_ - encode
- Form-urlencoded body encoder for OAuth token endpoints.
- [urlencoded](https://docs.rs/fn.urlencoded.html)
- Minimal percent-encoding for URL query parameters.

# solana_log_parser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-log-parser/0.1.0/solana_log_parser/

## Expand description

A parser for Solana transaction logs.

Solana runtime logs are a flat, ordered sequence of strings describing
program invocations, their nested inner instructions, and any messages
programs emit along the way (`msg!`, compute unit reports, return data,
etc). This crate turns that flat list into a tree of [ InstructionCall](https://docs.rs/struct.InstructionCall.html)s
that mirrors the actual call structure, so callers can walk invocations
and their children without re-parsing stack height markers themselves.

This crate is `no_std` (with `alloc`) so it can be used in constrained
environments such as on-chain programs or WASM.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let logs: Vec<String> = /* raw transaction logs */;
let instructions = Parser::parse(&logs)?;
for top_level in &instructions {
    for call in top_level.iter() {
        println!("{} at depth {}", call.program_id, call.stack_height);
    }
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Instruction](https://docs.rs/struct.InstructionCall.html)- Call
- A single program invocation, including any nested inner instructions it made and the logs it emitted.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineParser.html)- Parser
- Parses individual log lines that are known to belong to a specific program.
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html)
- Entry point for parsing raw transaction logs into a tree of
`InstructionCall`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorStatus.html)- Status
- Like `Status`
- [Line](https://docs.rs/enum.Line.html)
- The parsed classification of a single raw log line.
- [Log](https://docs.rs/enum.Log.html)
- One entry in an `InstructionCall`
- [LogHint](https://docs.rs/enum.LogHint.html)
- Categorizes what kind of program log a `Log::Program``Program log:`,`Program consumed`).
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur while parsing transaction logs.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)
- The outcome of a completed program invocation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- Parses a full list of transaction log lines into the top-level instructions (and their nested invocations) they describe.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_line.html)- line
- Classifies a single raw log line into a `Line`

# vec-arena 1.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/vec-arena/1.2.0

# vec-arena (deprecated)

**This crate is now deprecated in favor of  slab.**

#### What is this?

A simple object arena.

You want to build a doubly linked list? Or maybe a bidirectional tree? Perhaps an even more complicated object graph?

Managing ownership and lifetimes might be tough then. Your options boil down to:

- Use unsafe code to escape Rust's ownership rules.
- Wrap every object in `Rc<RefCell<T>>`.
- Use `Vec<T>`to store objects, then access them using indices.

If the last option seems most appealing to you, perhaps `Arena<T>` is for you.
It will provide a more convenient API than a plain `Vec<T>`.

#### Examples

Some data structures built using `Arena<T>`:

---

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/vec-arena/1.2.0/src/vec_arena/lib.rs.html

# vec_arena/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A simple object arena.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! `Arena<T>` is basically just a `Vec<Option<T>>`, which allows you to:
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! * Insert an object (reuse an existing [`None`] element, or append to the end).
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! * Remove object at a specified index.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! * Access object at a specified index.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! # Examples
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! Some data structures built using `Arena<T>`:
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! * [Doubly linked list](https://github.com/smol-rs/vec-arena/blob/master/examples/linked-list.rs)

[24](https://docs.rs#24)extern crate alloc;
[25](https://docs.rs#25)
[26](https://docs.rs#26)use alloc::fmt;
[27](https://docs.rs#27)use alloc::vec;
[28](https://docs.rs#28)use alloc::vec::Vec;
[29](https://docs.rs#29)use core::iter;
[30](https://docs.rs#30)use core::mem;
[31](https://docs.rs#31)use core::ops::{Index, IndexMut};

[33](https://docs.rs#33)
[34](https://docs.rs#34)/// A slot, which is either vacant or occupied.
[35](https://docs.rs#35)///
[36](https://docs.rs#36)/// Vacant slots in arena are linked together into a singly linked list. This allows the arena to
[37](https://docs.rs#37)/// efficiently find a vacant slot before inserting a new object, or reclaiming a slot after
[38](https://docs.rs#38)/// removing an object.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)#[derive(Clone)]
[40](https://docs.rs#40)enum Slot<T> {
[41](https://docs.rs#41)    /// Vacant slot, containing index to the next slot in the linked list.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)    Vacant(usize),
[43](https://docs.rs#43)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)    /// Occupied slot, containing a value.
[45](https://docs.rs#45)    Occupied(T),
[46](https://docs.rs#46)}
[47](https://docs.rs#47)
[48](https://docs.rs#48)impl<T> Slot<T> {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)    /// Returns `true` if the slot is vacant.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)    fn is_occupied(&self) -> bool {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)        match self {
[52](https://docs.rs#52)            Slot::Vacant(_) => false,
[53](https://docs.rs#53)            Slot::Occupied(_) => true,
[54](https://docs.rs#54)        }
[55](https://docs.rs#55)    }
[56](https://docs.rs#56)}
[57](https://docs.rs#57)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)/// An object arena.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)///
[60](https://docs.rs#60)/// `Arena<T>` holds an array of slots for storing objects.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// Every slot is always in one of two states: occupied or vacant.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)///
[63](https://docs.rs#63)/// Essentially, this is equivalent to `Vec<Option<T>>`.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)///
[65](https://docs.rs#65)/// # Insert and remove
[66](https://docs.rs#66)///
[67](https://docs.rs#67)/// When inserting a new object into arena, a vacant slot is found and then the object is placed
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// into the slot. If there are no vacant slots, the array is reallocated with bigger capacity.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)/// The cost of insertion is amortized `O(1)`.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)///
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// When removing an object, the slot containing it is marked as vacant and the object is returned.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)/// The cost of removal is `O(1)`.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)///
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// ```
[75](https://docs.rs#75)/// use vec_arena::Arena;
[76](https://docs.rs#76)///
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// let a = arena.insert(10);
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// let b = arena.insert(20);
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// assert_eq!(a, 0); // 10 was placed at index 0
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// assert_eq!(b, 1); // 20 was placed at index 1
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// assert_eq!(arena.remove(a), Some(10));
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// assert_eq!(arena.get(a), None); // slot at index 0 is now vacant
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// assert_eq!(arena.insert(30), 0); // slot at index 0 is reused
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// ```
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// # Indexing
[91](https://docs.rs#91)///
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// You can also access objects in an arena by index, just like you would in a [`Vec`].
[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// However, accessing a vacant slot by index or using an out-of-bounds index will result in panic.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)///
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// ```
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// use vec_arena::Arena;
[97](https://docs.rs#97)///
[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// let a = arena.insert(10);
[100](https://docs.rs#100)/// let b = arena.insert(20);
[101](https://docs.rs#101)///
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// assert_eq!(arena[a], 10);
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// assert_eq!(arena[b], 20);
[104](https://docs.rs#104)///
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// arena[a] += arena[b];
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// assert_eq!(arena[a], 30);
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// ```
[108](https://docs.rs#108)///
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// To access slots without fear of panicking, use [`get()`][`Arena::get()`] and
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// [`get_mut()`][`Arena::get_mut()`], which return [`Option`]s.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)pub struct Arena<T> {
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    /// Slots in which objects are stored.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    slots: Vec<Slot<T>>,
[114](https://docs.rs#114)
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    /// Number of occupied slots in the arena.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    len: usize,
[117](https://docs.rs#117)
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// Index of the first vacant slot in the linked list.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    head: usize,
[120](https://docs.rs#120)}
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)impl<T> Arena<T> {
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// Constructs a new, empty arena.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    ///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// The arena will not allocate until objects are inserted into it.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    ///
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// # Examples
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    ///
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    /// ```
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[131](https://docs.rs#131)    ///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    /// let mut arena: Arena<i32> = Arena::new();
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    /// ```
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    #[inline]
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    pub fn new() -> Self {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        Arena {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)            slots: Vec::new(),
[138](https://docs.rs#138)            len: 0,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)            head: !0,
[140](https://docs.rs#140)        }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    }
[142](https://docs.rs#142)
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// Constructs a new, empty arena with the specified capacity (number of slots).
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    ///
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    /// The arena will be able to hold exactly `cap` objects without reallocating.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// If `cap` is 0, the arena will not allocate.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    ///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// # Examples
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    ///
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// ```
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    ///
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    /// let mut arena = Arena::with_capacity(10);
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    ///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// assert_eq!(arena.len(), 0);
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    /// assert_eq!(arena.capacity(), 10);
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    ///
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    /// // These inserts are done without reallocating...
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    /// for i in 0..10 {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    ///     arena.insert(i);
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    /// }
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    /// assert_eq!(arena.capacity(), 10);
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    ///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// // ... but this one will reallocate.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// arena.insert(11);
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// assert!(arena.capacity() > 10);
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// ```
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    #[inline]
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    pub fn with_capacity(cap: usize) -> Self {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        Arena {
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            slots: Vec::with_capacity(cap),
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            len: 0,
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            head: !0,
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        }
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    }
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// Returns the number of slots in the arena.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    ///
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// # Examples
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    ///
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// ```
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    ///
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// let arena: Arena<i32> = Arena::with_capacity(10);
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// assert_eq!(arena.capacity(), 10);
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// ```
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    #[inline]
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    pub fn capacity(&self) -> usize {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        self.slots.capacity()
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    }
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// Returns the number of occupied slots in the arena.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    ///
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    /// # Examples
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    ///
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// ```
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    ///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// assert_eq!(arena.len(), 0);
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    ///
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// for i in 0..10 {
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    ///     arena.insert(());
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    ///     assert_eq!(arena.len(), i + 1);
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    /// }
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// ```
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    #[inline]
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        self.len
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    }
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// Returns `true` if all slots are vacant.
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    ///
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// # Examples
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    ///
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// ```
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    ///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// assert!(arena.is_empty());
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    ///
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    /// arena.insert(1);
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// assert!(!arena.is_empty());
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// ```
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    #[inline]
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        self.len == 0
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    }
[229](https://docs.rs#229)
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// Returns the index of the slot that next [`insert`][`Arena::insert()`] will use if no
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// mutating calls take place in between.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    ///
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// # Examples
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    ///
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// ```
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    ///
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    ///
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// let a = arena.next_vacant();
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// let b = arena.insert(1);
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    /// assert_eq!(a, b);
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// let c = arena.next_vacant();
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    /// let d = arena.insert(2);
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// assert_eq!(c, d);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// ```
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    #[inline]
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    pub fn next_vacant(&self) -> usize {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        if self.head == !0 {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            self.len
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        } else {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)            self.head
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    }
[255](https://docs.rs#255)
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// Inserts an object into the arena and returns the slot index it was stored in.
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    ///
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    /// The arena will reallocate if it's full.
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    ///
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// # Examples
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    ///
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// ```
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    ///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// let a = arena.insert(1);
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    /// let b = arena.insert(2);
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// assert!(a != b);
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// ```
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    #[inline]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    pub fn insert(&mut self, object: T) -> usize {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        self.len += 1;
[274](https://docs.rs#274)
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        if self.head == !0 {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)            self.slots.push(Slot::Occupied(object));
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            self.len - 1
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        } else {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)            let index = self.head;
[280](https://docs.rs#280)            match self.slots[index] {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)                Slot::Vacant(next) => {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)                    self.head = next;
[283](https://docs.rs#283)                    self.slots[index] = Slot::Occupied(object);
[284](https://docs.rs#284)                }
[285](https://docs.rs#285)                Slot::Occupied(_) => unreachable!(),
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            index
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        }
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    /// Removes the object stored at `index` from the arena and returns it.
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    ///
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    /// If the slot is vacant or `index` is out of bounds, [`None`] will be returned.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    ///
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// # Examples
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    ///
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    /// ```
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// let a = arena.insert("hello");
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    ///
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// assert_eq!(arena.len(), 1);
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// assert_eq!(arena.remove(a), Some("hello"));
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// assert_eq!(arena.len(), 0);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// assert_eq!(arena.remove(a), None);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// ```
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    #[inline]
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    pub fn remove(&mut self, index: usize) -> Option<T> {
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        match self.slots.get_mut(index) {
[312](https://docs.rs#312)            None => None,
[313](https://docs.rs#313)            Some(&mut Slot::Vacant(_)) => None,
[314](https://docs.rs#314)            Some(slot @ &mut Slot::Occupied(_)) => {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)                if let Slot::Occupied(object) = mem::replace(slot, Slot::Vacant(self.head)) {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)                    self.head = index;
[317](https://docs.rs#317)                    self.len -= 1;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)                    Some(object)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)                } else {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)                    unreachable!();
[321](https://docs.rs#321)                }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)            }
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// Retains objects for which the closure returns `true`.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    ///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    /// All other objects will be removed from the arena.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    ///
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    /// # Examples
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    ///
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    /// ```
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    ///
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    ///
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// let a = arena.insert(0);
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// let b = arena.insert(1);
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// let c = arena.insert(2);
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    ///
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// arena.retain(|k, v| k == a || *v == 1);
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    ///
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// assert!(arena.get(a).is_some());
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// assert!(arena.get(b).is_some());
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// assert!(arena.get(c).is_none());
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    /// ```
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    pub fn retain<F>(&mut self, mut f: F)
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    where
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        F: FnMut(usize, &mut T) -> bool,
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        for i in 0..self.slots.len() {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            if let Slot::Occupied(v) = &mut self.slots[i] {
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                if !f(i, v) {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)                    self.remove(i);
[355](https://docs.rs#355)                }
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            }
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        }
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// Clears the arena, removing and dropping all objects it holds.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    ///
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// Keeps the allocated memory for reuse.
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    ///
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// # Examples
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// ```
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    ///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// for i in 0..10 {
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    ///     arena.insert(i);
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// }
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    ///
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// assert_eq!(arena.len(), 10);
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// arena.clear();
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// assert_eq!(arena.len(), 0);
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// ```
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    #[inline]
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    pub fn clear(&mut self) {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        self.slots.clear();
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        self.len = 0;
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        self.head = !0;
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    }
[384](https://docs.rs#384)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// Returns a reference to the object stored at `index`.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// If the slot is vacant or `index` is out of bounds, [`None`] will be returned.
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    ///
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// # Examples
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    ///
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    /// ```
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    ///
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// let index = arena.insert("hello");
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    ///
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// assert_eq!(arena.get(index), Some(&"hello"));
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// arena.remove(index);
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// assert_eq!(arena.get(index), None);
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// ```
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    #[inline]
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    pub fn get(&self, index: usize) -> Option<&T> {
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        match self.slots.get(index) {
[404](https://docs.rs#404)            None => None,
[405](https://docs.rs#405)            Some(&Slot::Vacant(_)) => None,
[406](https://docs.rs#406)            Some(&Slot::Occupied(ref object)) => Some(object),
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        }
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    }
[409](https://docs.rs#409)
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// Returns a mutable reference to the object stored at `index`.
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// If the slot is vacant or `index` is out of bounds, [`None`] will be returned.
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    ///
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// # Examples
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    ///
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// ```
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    ///
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// let index = arena.insert(7);
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    ///
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    /// assert_eq!(arena.get_mut(index), Some(&mut 7));
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// *arena.get_mut(index).unwrap() *= 10;
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// assert_eq!(arena.get_mut(index), Some(&mut 70));
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// ```
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    #[inline]
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    pub fn get_mut(&mut self, index: usize) -> Option<&mut T> {
[428](https://docs.rs#428)        match self.slots.get_mut(index) {
[429](https://docs.rs#429)            None => None,
[430](https://docs.rs#430)            Some(&mut Slot::Vacant(_)) => None,
[431](https://docs.rs#431)            Some(&mut Slot::Occupied(ref mut object)) => Some(object),
[432](https://docs.rs#432)        }
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    }
[434](https://docs.rs#434)
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// Swaps two objects in the arena.
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    ///
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// The two indices are `a` and `b`.
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    ///
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// # Panics
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    ///
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// Panics if any of the indices is out of bounds or any of the slots is vacant.
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    ///
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    /// # Examples
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    ///
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    /// ```
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    ///
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// let a = arena.insert(7);
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    /// let b = arena.insert(8);
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    ///
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// arena.swap(a, b);
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// assert_eq!(arena.get(a), Some(&8));
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// assert_eq!(arena.get(b), Some(&7));
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    /// ```
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    #[inline]
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    pub fn swap(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) {
[458](https://docs.rs#458)        assert!(self.slots[a].is_occupied(), "invalid object ID");
[459](https://docs.rs#459)        assert!(self.slots[b].is_occupied(), "invalid object ID");
[460](https://docs.rs#460)
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        if a != b {
[462](https://docs.rs#462)            let (a, b) = (a.min(b), a.max(b));
[463](https://docs.rs#463)            let (l, r) = self.slots.split_at_mut(b);
[464](https://docs.rs#464)            mem::swap(&mut l[a], &mut r[0]);
[465](https://docs.rs#465)        }
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    }
[467](https://docs.rs#467)
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    /// Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more objects to be inserted.
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    ///
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    /// The arena may reserve more space to avoid frequent reallocations.
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    ///
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    /// # Panics
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    ///
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    /// Panics if the new capacity overflows `usize`.
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    ///
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// # Examples
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    ///
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    /// ```
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    ///
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    /// arena.insert("hello");
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    ///
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    /// arena.reserve(10);
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    /// assert!(arena.capacity() >= 11);
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    /// ```
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    pub fn reserve(&mut self, additional: usize) {
[488](https://docs.rs#488)        let vacant = self.slots.len() - self.len;
[489](https://docs.rs#489)        if additional > vacant {
[490](https://docs.rs#490)            self.slots.reserve(additional - vacant);
[491](https://docs.rs#491)        }
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    }
[493](https://docs.rs#493)
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    /// Reserves the minimum capacity for exactly `additional` more objects to be inserted.
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    ///
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    /// Note that the allocator may give the arena more space than it requests.
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    ///
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// # Panics
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    ///
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    /// Panics if the new capacity overflows `usize`.
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    ///
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    /// # Examples
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    ///
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    /// ```
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    /// use vec_arena::Arena;
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    ///
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    /// let mut arena = Arena::new();
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    /// arena.insert("hello");
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    ///
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    /// arena.reserve_exact(10);
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// assert!(arena.capacity() >= 11);
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    /// ```
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    pub fn reserve_exact(&mut self, additional: usize) {
[514](https://docs.rs#514)        let vacant = self.slots.len() - self.len;
[515](https://docs.rs#515)        if additional > vacant {
[516](https://docs.rs#516)            self.slots.reserve_exact(additional - vacant);
[517](https://docs.rs#517)        }
[518](https://docs.rs#518)    }
[519](https://docs.rs#519)
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    /// Returns an iterator over occupied slots.
