# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize JSON data to a Rust data structure.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- When serializing or deserializing JSON goes wrong.

- A map of String to serde_json::Value.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)- `std`

- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)
- The Value enum, a loosely typed way of representing any valid JSON value.

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)
- Create a new temporary file or directory with custom options.
- [Named](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)- Temp - File
- A named temporary file.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.PathPersistError.html)- Persist - Error
- Error returned when persisting a temporary file path fails.
- [Persist](https://docs.rs/struct.PersistError.html)- Error
- Error returned when persisting a temporary file fails.
- [Spooled](https://docs.rs/struct.SpooledTempFile.html)- Temp - File
- An object that behaves like a regular temporary file, but keeps data in memory until it reaches a configured size, at which point the data is written to a temporary file on disk, and further operations use the file on disk.
- [TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)
- A directory in the filesystem that is automatically deleted when it goes out of scope.
- [Temp](https://docs.rs/struct.TempPath.html)- Path

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [spooled_](https://docs.rs/fn.spooled_tempfile.html)- tempfile
- Create a new `SpooledTempFile``spooled_tempfile_in`
- [spooled_](https://docs.rs/fn.spooled_tempfile_in.html)- tempfile_ - in

- [tempdir](https://docs.rs/fn.tempdir.html)
- Create a new temporary directory. Also see `tempdir_in`

# calib_targets - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/calib-targets/0.10.0/target-redirect/calib_targets/

## Expand description

High-level facade crate for the `calib-targets-*` workspace.

This crate provides:

- stable, convenient re-exports of the underlying detector crates
- (feature-gated) end-to-end helpers that run a ChESS corner detector
(`chess-corners`) and then run a target detector on an image or raw buffer.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets::detect;
use calib_targets::chessboard::DetectorParams;
use image::ImageReader;
let img = ImageReader::open("board.png")?.decode()?.to_luma8();
let params = DetectorParams::default();
let result = detect::detect_chessboard(&img, &detect::default_chess_config(), ¶ms);
println!("detected: {}", result.is_some());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#python-bindings)Python bindings

Python bindings live in `crates/calib-targets-py` and expose the
`calib_targets` module. See `crates/calib-targets-py/README.md` in the
repository for setup, the `detect_*` APIs, and printable-target generation.
Config inputs accept typed Python classes; `detect_charuco` requires
`params` with `params.board`. For marker boards, `target_position` is
populated only when `params.layout.cell_size` is provided and alignment
succeeds.

[§](https://docs.rs#api-map)API map

- `calib_targets::core`: core types (corners, grids, homographies, images).
- `calib_targets::chessboard`: chessboard detection from ChESS corners.
- `calib_targets::aruco`: ArUco/AprilTag dictionaries and marker decoding.
- `calib_targets::charuco`: ChArUco board alignment and IDs.
- `calib_targets::puzzleboard`: PuzzleBoard edge-code decoding and IDs.
- `calib_targets::marker`: checkerboard + circle marker boards.
- `calib_targets::printable`: printable target generation and JSON/SVG/PNG output.
- `calib_targets::detect`(feature- `image`): end-to-end helpers from- `image::GrayImage`.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

Benchmarks are coming. The goal is to be the fastest detector in this class while maintaining high sensitivity and accuracy.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [calib_targets_aruco](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-aruco/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_aruco/index.html)as aruco;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_charuco](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-charuco/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_charuco/index.html)as charuco;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_chessboard](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-chessboard/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_chessboard/index.html)as chessboard;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_core](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_core/index.html)as core;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_marker](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-marker/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_marker/index.html)as marker;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_print](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-print/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_print/index.html)as printable;
- `pub use`- [calib_targets_puzzleboard](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-puzzleboard/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_puzzleboard/index.html)as puzzleboard;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chess](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessCorner.html)- Corner
- Canonical 2D corner consumed by the chessboard detector.
- [Coord](https://docs.rs/struct.Coord.html)
- Integer coordinate on a lattice.
- [Labeled](https://docs.rs/struct.LabeledCorner.html)- Corner
- A corner that is part of a detected target, with optional ID info.
- [Target](https://docs.rs/struct.TargetDetection.html)- Detection
- One detected target (board instance) in an image.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.TargetKind.html)- Kind
- The kind of target that a detection corresponds to.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets/0.10.0/src/calib_targets/lib.rs.html

# calib_targets/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! High-level facade crate for the `calib-targets-*` workspace.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This crate provides:
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! - stable, convenient re-exports of the underlying detector crates
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! - (feature-gated) end-to-end helpers that run a ChESS corner detector
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!   (`chess-corners`) and then run a target detector on an image or raw buffer.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! ## Quickstart
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! ```no_run
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! use calib_targets::detect;
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! use calib_targets::chessboard::DetectorParams;
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! use image::ImageReader;
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! let img = ImageReader::open("board.png")?.decode()?.to_luma8();
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! let params = DetectorParams::default();
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! let result = detect::detect_chessboard(&img, &detect::default_chess_config(), ¶ms);
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! println!("detected: {}", result.is_some());
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! # Ok(())
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! # }
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! ```
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! ## Python bindings
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! Python bindings live in `crates/calib-targets-py` and expose the
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! `calib_targets` module. See `crates/calib-targets-py/README.md` in the
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! repository for setup, the `detect_*` APIs, and printable-target generation.
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! Config inputs accept typed Python classes; `detect_charuco` requires
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! `params` with `params.board`. For marker boards, `target_position` is
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! populated only when `params.layout.cell_size` is provided and alignment
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! succeeds.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ## API map
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! - `calib_targets::core`: core types (corners, grids, homographies, images).
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! - `calib_targets::chessboard`: chessboard detection from ChESS corners.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! - `calib_targets::aruco`: ArUco/AprilTag dictionaries and marker decoding.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! - `calib_targets::charuco`: ChArUco board alignment and IDs.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! - `calib_targets::puzzleboard`: PuzzleBoard edge-code decoding and IDs.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! - `calib_targets::marker`: checkerboard + circle marker boards.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! - `calib_targets::printable`: printable target generation and JSON/SVG/PNG output.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! - `calib_targets::detect` (feature `image`): end-to-end helpers from `image::GrayImage`.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! ## Performance
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! Benchmarks are coming. The goal is to be the fastest detector in this class
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! while maintaining high sensitivity and accuracy.
[49](https://docs.rs#49)#![deny(missing_docs)]
[50](https://docs.rs#50)
[51](https://docs.rs#51)pub use calib_targets_aruco as aruco;
[52](https://docs.rs#52)pub use calib_targets_charuco as charuco;
[53](https://docs.rs#53)pub use calib_targets_chessboard as chessboard;
[54](https://docs.rs#54)pub use calib_targets_core as core;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)pub use calib_targets_marker as marker;
[56](https://docs.rs#56)pub use calib_targets_print as printable;
[57](https://docs.rs#57)pub use calib_targets_puzzleboard as puzzleboard;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)
[59](https://docs.rs#59)pub use calib_targets_chessboard::ChessCorner;
[60](https://docs.rs#60)pub use calib_targets_core::{Coord, LabeledCorner, TargetDetection, TargetKind};
[61](https://docs.rs#61)

# calib_targets_aruco - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-aruco/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_aruco/index.html

## Expand description

ArUco/AprilTag marker dictionaries and decoding utilities.

This crate focuses on:

- embedded built-in dictionaries (compiled into the binary),
- matching observed marker codes against those dictionaries,
- decoding markers either from rectified grids or from per-cell image quads.

It does **not** perform quad detection. Instead, it expects a grid model
(for example from `calib-targets-chessboard`) or explicit cell corners.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_aruco::{
    builtins, scan_decode_markers, GrayImageView, Matcher, ScanDecodeConfig,
};
let dict = builtins::builtin_dictionary("DICT_4X4_50").expect("dict");
let matcher = Matcher::new(dict, 1);
let pixels = vec![0u8; 16 * 16];
let view = GrayImageView {
    width: 16,
    height: 16,
    data: &pixels,
};
let scan_cfg = ScanDecodeConfig::default();
let markers = scan_decode_markers(&view, 4, 4, 4.0, &scan_cfg, &matcher);
println!("markers: {}", markers.len());
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [builtins](https://docs.rs/builtins/index.html)
- Embedded built-in dictionaries.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Aruco](https://docs.rs/struct.ArucoScanConfig.html)- Scan - Config
- Optional overrides for marker scanning and matching.
- [Cell](https://docs.rs/struct.CellSamples.html)- Samples
- Rectified per-cell intensity samples suitable for custom match scoring.
- [Dictionary](https://docs.rs/struct.Dictionary.html)
- A fixed ArUco/AprilTag-style dictionary.
- [Gray](https://docs.rs/struct.GrayImageView.html)- Image - View
- Borrowed view over an 8-bit grayscale image.
- [Marker](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkerCell.html)- Cell
- One square cell with its image-space corners.
- [Marker](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkerDetection.html)- Detection
- One decoded marker detection.
- [Match](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)
- A dictionary match for an observed marker code.
- [Matcher](https://docs.rs/struct.Matcher.html)
- Matcher for a fixed dictionary.
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/struct.ScanDecodeConfig.html)- Decode - Config
- Decoder configuration for scanning markers.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Dictionary](https://docs.rs/enum.DictionaryError.html)- Error
- Validation error returned by `Dictionary::from_static_codes`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_marker_in_cell.html)- marker_ - in_ - cell
- Decode a single marker from one square cell in image space.
- [rotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.rotate_code_u64.html)- code_ - u64
- Rotate a code stored in row-major bits: `idx = y * N + x`.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_cell.html)- cell
- Sample a rectified per-cell intensity grid from an image using a cell quad, without decoding any marker id.
- [scan_](https://docs.rs/fn.scan_decode_markers.html)- decode_ - markers
- Scan all square cells `(sx,sy)`in`0..cells_x × 0..cells_y`, read + decode markers.
- [scan_](https://docs.rs/fn.scan_decode_markers_in_cells.html)- decode_ - markers_ - in_ - cells
- Decode markers from explicit per-cell image quads.

# calib_targets_charuco - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-charuco/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_charuco/index.html

## Expand description

ChArUco-related utilities.

Current focus:

- chessboard detection from ChESS corners,
- per-cell marker decoding (no full-image warp by default),
- alignment to a known board definition and corner ID assignment.

Marker dictionaries and decoding live in `calib-targets-aruco`.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_charuco::{
    builtins, CharucoBoardSpec, CharucoDetector, CharucoParams, ChessCorner,
    GrayImageView, MarkerLayout,
};
let board = CharucoBoardSpec::new(5, 7, 1.0, 0.7, builtins::DICT_4X4_50)
    .with_marker_layout(MarkerLayout::OpenCvCharuco);
let params = CharucoParams::for_board(&board);
let detector = CharucoDetector::new(params)?;
let pixels = vec![0u8; 32 * 32];
let view = GrayImageView {
    width: 32,
    height: 32,
    data: &pixels,
};
let corners: Vec<ChessCorner> = Vec::new();
let _ = detector.detect(&view, &corners)?;
```

# calib_targets_chessboard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-chessboard/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_chessboard/index.html

## Expand description

Invariant-first chessboard detector.

Takes a slice of [ChESS](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/research/rainbow/projects/chess/)
X-junction corners and returns an integer-labelled chessboard grid. The
crate’s only output contract is: *every labelled corner has been proven
to sit at a real grid intersection.* Missing corners are acceptable;
wrong corners are not.

**High detection rate on our private regression set with zero wrong
 (i, j) labels** (non-negligible lens distortion and motion blur).

Algorithm reference: see `book/src/chessboard.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline)Pipeline

The detector builds its `(i, j)` labelling with the **topological** grid
finder in [ projective_grid](https://docs.rs/projective-grid/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/projective_grid/index.html) (a Delaunay triangulation + an axis-driven
cell test), then runs a chessboard-specific recovery + precision pass over
the labelled components:

| Stage | Name | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `prefilter` | Drop corners failing strength / fit-quality / axes-validity gates. |
| 2 | `cluster_axes` | Recover the two global grid-direction centres `{Θ₀, Θ₁}`via histogram + 2-means; label each corner as canonical or swapped. |
| 3 | `topological_grid` | Delaunay + axis-driven cell test → connected labelled `(i, j)`components ().`projective_grid::detect_grid_all` |
| 4 | `recover_components` | Per-component recall boosters (interior gap fill + line extrapolation with a directional edge scale) + shared component merge. |
| 5 | `final_geometry_check` | Mandatory precision gate: line collinearity + local-H residual + direct wrong-label check + largest cardinal component. Can only drop corners; never adds. |
| 6 | `output` | Labelled grid → canonicalised, non-negative-rebased .`ChessboardDetection` |

Each stage is its own module or function; see the submodules.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_chessboard::{ChessCorner, Detector, DetectorParams};
use calib_targets_core::AxisEstimate;
use nalgebra::Point2;
// A synthetic 7×7 chessboard corner cloud at 20 px pitch. Adjacent
// corners carry opposite axis-slot orderings (the parity invariant).
let mut corners: Vec<ChessCorner> = Vec::new();
for j in 0..7 {
    for i in 0..7 {
        let swapped = (i + j) % 2 == 1;
        let (a0, a1) = if swapped {
            (std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_2, 0.0)
        } else {
            (0.0, std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_2)
        };
        corners.push(ChessCorner {
            position: Point2::new(i as f32 * 20.0 + 50.0, j as f32 * 20.0 + 50.0),
            axes: [
                AxisEstimate { angle: a0, sigma: 0.01 },
                AxisEstimate { angle: a1, sigma: 0.01 },
            ],
            contrast: 10.0,
            fit_rms: 1.0,
            // Above the default `min_corner_strength` floor (33.0).
            strength: 100.0,
        });
    }
}
let det = Detector::new(DetectorParams::default()).expect("default params are valid");
let detection = det.detect(&corners).expect("clean 7×7 grid detects");
assert_eq!(detection.corners.len(), 49);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rectification-helpers)Rectification helpers

Two rectifiers are exposed: [ rectify_from_chessboard_result](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_from_chessboard_result.html)
(

[) and](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedBoardView.html)

`RectifiedBoardView`[(](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_mesh_from_grid.html)

`rectify_mesh_from_grid`[). The former takes a](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedMeshView.html)

`RectifiedMeshView`[directly; the latter is pattern-agnostic and takes a](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessboardDetection.html)

`ChessboardDetection``&[LabeledCorner]` plus an inlier index list. Both produce a
rectified view and can be used with any consistent `(i, j)`
labelling.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Advanced](https://docs.rs/struct.AdvancedTuning.html)- Tuning
- Advanced, **unstable**per-stage tuning knobs for the chessboard detector.
- [Chess](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessCorner.html)- Corner
- Canonical 2D corner consumed by the chessboard detector.
- [Chessboard](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessboardCorner.html)- Corner
- A single labelled chessboard corner.
- [Chessboard](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessboardDetection.html)- Detection
- Result of chessboard detection: the labelled corner set.
- [Detector](https://docs.rs/struct.Detector.html)
- Top-level detector.
- [Detector](https://docs.rs/struct.DetectorParams.html)- Params
- Top-level detector configuration.
- [Rectified](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedBoardView.html)- Board - View
- A rectified, fronto-parallel view of a detected chessboard.
- [Rectified](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedMeshView.html)- Mesh - View
- A fronto-parallel mesh rectification of a labelled chessboard grid.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [detect_](https://docs.rs/fn.detect_all_topological.html)- all_ - topological
- Run the topological pipeline and return one `ChessboardDetection`
- [rectify_](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_from_chessboard_result.html)- from_ - chessboard_ - result
- Rectify a chessboard from a `ChessboardDetection`
- [rectify_](https://docs.rs/fn.rectify_mesh_from_grid.html)- mesh_ - from_ - grid
- Build a rectified “board view” by piecewise homographies per grid cell. This is robust to lens distortion because it does not assume a single global H.
- [trace_](https://docs.rs/fn.trace_topological.html)- topological
- Run the same topological input adaptation as `detect_all_topological`

# calib_targets_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_core/index.html

## Expand description

Core types and utilities for calibration target detection.

This crate is intentionally small and purely geometric. It does *not*
depend on any concrete corner detector implementation or image type, but it
owns the shared detector configuration contracts used across the workspace.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_core::{LabeledCorner, TargetDetection, TargetKind};
use nalgebra::Point2;
let corner = LabeledCorner::new(Point2::new(12.0, 8.0), 0.9);
let detection = TargetDetection::new(TargetKind::Chessboard, vec![corner]);
println!("{}", detection.corners.len());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#includes)Includes

- Homography estimation and warping helpers.
- Lightweight grayscale image views and sampling.
- Grid alignment and target detection types.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Shared JSON IO helpers for config and report types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Axis](https://docs.rs/struct.AxisEstimate.html)- Estimate
- Local estimate of one undirected grid axis at a detected corner.
- [Coord](https://docs.rs/struct.Coord.html)
- The canonical integer grid-coordinate type `(u, v)`—`u`is the grid’s first axis (right),`v`the second (down). Re-exported from`projective_grid`
- [Detector](https://docs.rs/struct.DetectorConfig.html)- Config
- High-level detection configuration.
- [Gray](https://docs.rs/struct.GrayImage.html)- Image
- Owned 8-bit grayscale image.
- [Gray](https://docs.rs/struct.GrayImageView.html)- Image - View
- Borrowed view over an 8-bit grayscale image.
- [Grid](https://docs.rs/struct.GridAlignment.html)- Alignment
- A grid alignment: `dst = transform(src) + translation`.
- [Grid](https://docs.rs/struct.GridTransform.html)- Transform
- Integer 2D grid transform (a 2×2 matrix) for aligning detected grids to a board model.
- [Homography](https://docs.rs/struct.Homography.html)
- A 3×3 projective homography matrix.
- [Homography](https://docs.rs/struct.HomographyQuality.html)- Quality
- Numerical quality of a homography matrix.
- [Labeled](https://docs.rs/struct.LabeledCorner.html)- Corner
- A corner that is part of a detected target, with optional ID info.
- [Rectified](https://docs.rs/struct.RectifiedView.html)- View
- A rectified (fronto-parallel) view of a detected board, plus the mapping back to the original image.
- [Target](https://docs.rs/struct.TargetDetection.html)- Detection
- One detected target (board instance) in an image.

- [Orientation](https://docs.rs/enum.OrientationMethod.html)- Method
- Method used to fit the two grid axes at a detected corner.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [axis_](https://docs.rs/fn.axis_estimate_from_next.html)- estimate_ - from_ - next
- Project a `NextLocalAxis`
- [axis_](https://docs.rs/fn.axis_estimate_to_next.html)- estimate_ - to_ - next
- Promote `AxisEstimate``projective_grid`
- [cell_](https://docs.rs/fn.cell_rect_corners_at.html)- rect_ - corners_ - at
- The four corners of a unit grid cell at `gc`, in canonical rectified space, in clockwise**TL, TR, BR, BL**order (the workspace-wide quad/homography order).
- [complete_](https://docs.rs/fn.complete_cell_corners.html)- cell_ - corners
- The four image corners of the unit cell whose top-left intersection is grid
`(u, v)`, in**TL, TR, BR, BL**order (clockwise — the canonical quad order used for every homography fit in the workspace). Returns`None`if any of the cell’s four grid intersections is absent from the map.
- [corner_](https://docs.rs/fn.corner_map_bounds.html)- map_ - bounds
- Inclusive grid-coordinate bounds `(min_u, min_v, max_u, max_v)`over a corner map’s keys, or`None`when the map is empty.
- [estimate_](https://docs.rs/fn.estimate_homography_rect_to_img.html)- homography_ - rect_ - to_ - img
- Estimate H such that `p_dst ~ H * p_src`from N >= 4 point correspondences.
- [estimate_](https://docs.rs/fn.estimate_homography_with_quality.html)- homography_ - with_ - quality
- Estimate H such that `p_dst ~ H * p_src`from N >= 4 point correspondences, returning the matrix together with its`HomographyQuality`
- [grid_](https://docs.rs/fn.grid_transform_from_next.html)- transform_ - from_ - next
- Project a `NextGridTransform`
- [grid_](https://docs.rs/fn.grid_transform_to_next.html)- transform_ - to_ - next
- Convert the legacy `GridTransform`into a tagged square-lattice transform for`projective_grid`
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_from_4pt.html)- from_ - 4pt
- Compute H from exactly 4 point correspondences: `dst ~ H * src`.
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_from_4pt_with_quality.html)- from_ - 4pt_ - with_ - quality
- 4-point variant of `estimate_homography_with_quality`
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_from_next.html)- from_ - next
- Project a `Projective2<f32>``Homography`
- [homography_](https://docs.rs/fn.homography_to_next.html)- to_ - next
- Convert `Homography`
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_tracing.html)- tracing
- Install a global `tracing`subscriber (available with the`tracing`feature).
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_with_level.html)- with_ - level
- Install the simple logger with the provided level filter.
- [log_](https://docs.rs/fn.log_sigmoid.html)- sigmoid
- Numerically stable `log(sigmoid(x))`.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_bilinear.html)- bilinear
- Bilinearly sample a grayscale image at sub-pixel `(x, y)`.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_bilinear_fast.html)- bilinear_ - fast
- Bilinearly sample a grayscale image, skipping bounds checks on the hot path.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/fn.sample_bilinear_u8.html)- bilinear_ - u8
- Bilinearly sample a grayscale image and round the result to `u8`.
- [square_](https://docs.rs/fn.square_predict_grid_position.html)- predict_ - grid_ - position
- Predict a square-grid corner position from complete cardinal neighbor pairs.
- [warp_](https://docs.rs/fn.warp_perspective_gray.html)- perspective_ - gray
- Warp into a rectified image: for each destination pixel center, map to
source image coordinates via `H_img_from_rect`and bilinear-sample.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Corner](https://docs.rs/type.CornerMap.html)- Map
- A grid → image corner map: integer grid intersections to their sub-pixel image positions. The shared currency of the marker / ChArUco square-cell warp paths.

# calib_targets_marker - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets-marker/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_marker/index.html

## Expand description

Checkerboard marker target detector (checkerboard + 3 circles in the middle).

Pipeline overview:

- Detect a chessboard grid from ChESS corners (partial boards are allowed).
- Score circular markers per-cell in image space.
- Match circle candidates to the known layout and estimate the grid offset.
- Return typed marker-board corners with optional board alignment.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use calib_targets_chessboard::ChessCorner;
use calib_targets_core::GrayImageView;
use calib_targets_marker::{
    CellCoords, CirclePolarity, MarkerBoardDetector, MarkerBoardSpec, MarkerBoardParams,
    MarkerCircleSpec,
};
let layout = MarkerBoardSpec::new(
    6,
    8,
    [
        MarkerCircleSpec::new(CellCoords { i: 2, j: 2 }, CirclePolarity::White),
        MarkerCircleSpec::new(CellCoords { i: 3, j: 2 }, CirclePolarity::Black),
        MarkerCircleSpec::new(CellCoords { i: 2, j: 3 }, CirclePolarity::White),
    ],
)
.with_cell_size(1.0);
let params = MarkerBoardParams::new(layout);
let detector = MarkerBoardDetector::new(params).expect("valid chessboard config");
let pixels = vec![0u8; 32 * 32];
let view = GrayImageView {
    width: 32,
    height: 32,
    data: &pixels,
};
let corners: Vec<ChessCorner> = Vec::new();
let _ = detector.detect_from_image_and_corners(&view, &corners);
```

- Integer translation between detected grid cells and board cells.

- Canonical 2D corner consumed by the chessboard detector.

- Tuning knobs for per-cell circular-marker scoring.

- Integer 2D grid transform (a 2×2 matrix) for aligning detected grids to a board model.

- Detection report for serialization.

- Marker board detector: chessboard + three circle markers.

- Parameters for marker-board detection.
- [Marker](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkerBoardSpec.html)- Board - Spec
- Fixed marker board layout: chessboard size plus 3 circle markers.
- [Marker](https://docs.rs/struct.MarkerCircleSpec.html)- Circle - Spec
- One expected marker circle on the board.

# calib_targets::generate - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets/0.10.0/calib_targets/generate/index.html

## Expand description

Ergonomic constructors for printable-target documents.

Thin wrappers over [ PrintableTargetDocument::new](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-print/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_print/model/struct.PrintableTargetDocument.html#method.new)
that hide the

`TargetSpec` enum wrapping. The returned document uses default
[(A4 portrait, 10 mm margins) and default](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-print/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_print/model/page/struct.PageSpec.html)

`PageSpec`[(300 DPI, no debug annotations); callers mutate the returned document’s](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-print/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_print/model/page/struct.RenderOptions.html)

`RenderOptions``page` / `render` fields for customisation.```
use calib_targets::generate::chessboard_document;
use calib_targets::printable::{write_target_bundle, PageSize, PageOrientation};
let mut doc = chessboard_document(6, 8, 20.0);
doc.page.size = PageSize::Letter;
doc.page.orientation = PageOrientation::Landscape;
let bundle = write_target_bundle(&doc, "my_board")?;
println!("{}", bundle.json_path.display());
```

# ChessCorner in calib_targets - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets/0.10.0/calib_targets/struct.ChessCorner.html

```
pub struct ChessCorner {
    pub position:
```
[OPoint](https://docs.rs/nalgebra/0.34.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/nalgebra/geometry/point/struct.OPoint.html)<[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), [Const](https://docs.rs/nalgebra/0.34.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/nalgebra/base/dimension/struct.Const.html)<2>>,
    pub axes: [[AxisEstimate](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_core/corner/struct.AxisEstimate.html); [2](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)],
    pub contrast: [f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html),
    pub fit_rms: [f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html),
    pub strength: [f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html),
}## Expand description

Canonical 2D corner consumed by the chessboard detector.

Carries the per-corner data the pipeline needs to admit or reject the
corner during clustering, seed selection, grow, and post-grow validation:
pixel position, the two local grid-axis directions with per-axis 1σ
uncertainty, the ChESS detector’s response (`strength`), the tanh-fit
`contrast` amplitude, and the tanh-fit residual (`fit_rms`).

Callers constructing corners from `chess_corners::CornerDescriptor` typically
go through the workspace facade’s adapter; callers handing the detector a
pre-built corner cloud (tests, custom upstreams) construct `ChessCorner`
directly.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.position)

`position: `[OPoint](https://docs.rs/nalgebra/0.34.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/nalgebra/geometry/point/struct.OPoint.html)<[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), [Const](https://docs.rs/nalgebra/0.34.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/nalgebra/base/dimension/struct.Const.html)<2>>Corner position in pixel coordinates.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.axes)

`axes: [`[AxisEstimate](https://docs.rs/calib-targets-core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/calib_targets_core/corner/struct.AxisEstimate.html); [2](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)]Two local grid-axis directions with per-axis 1σ angular uncertainty.
Default-constructed axes carry `sigma = π` (“no information”) and
cause the corner to be skipped by every axis-aware stage.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.contrast)

`contrast: `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)Bright/dark amplitude `|A|` (≥ 0, gray levels) from the upstream
two-axis tanh fit. Independent from [ Self::strength](https://docs.rs/struct.ChessCorner.html#structfield.strength).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.fit_rms)

`fit_rms: `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)RMS residual of the two-axis intensity fit (gray levels). Lower is a tighter match to an ideal chessboard corner.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.strength)

`strength: `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)Corner detector response (raw ChESS response at the detected peak). Positive values are corner candidates.

# Coord in calib_targets - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/calib-targets/0.10.0/calib_targets/struct.Coord.html

## Expand description

Integer coordinate on a lattice.

For square grids this is `(u, v) = (i, j)`. For hex grids this is axial
`(u, v) = (q, r)`.

This is the canonical integer grid-coordinate type for the whole
calibration-target workspace; it serializes as a `{ "u", "v" }` object.

## Fields (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

## This struct is marked as non-exhaustive

`Struct { .. }` syntax; cannot be matched against without a wildcard `..`; and struct update syntax will not work.[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.u)

`u: `[i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)First lattice coordinate: square `i`, or hex axial `q`.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.v)

`v: `[i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)Second lattice coordinate: square `j`, or hex axial `r`.

## This struct is marked as non-exhaustive

Non-exhaustive structs could have additional fields added in future. Therefore, non-exhaustive structs cannot be constructed in external crates using the traditional

`Struct { .. }` syntax; cannot be matched against without a wildcard `..`; and struct update syntax will not work.[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.kind)

# yatrosci-bio-systems 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yatrosci-bio-systems/0.1.0

# SciRS Systems Biology (Advanced)

Formal modeling of biological networks and systems. No simplified equations.

This crate provides:

- Mass-action kinetics (law of mass action, reaction order)
- Metabolic Control Analysis (MCA) (Elasticities, Control coefficients)
- Stoichiometric Modeling (Flux Balance Analysis foundations)
- Gene Regulatory Networks (Hill kinetics, cooperativity, Hill plot)

# References

- Hill, A. V. (1910). The possible effects of the aggregation of the
molecules of haemoglobin on its dissociation curves.
*J. Physiol.*40, iv–vii.
- Guldberg, C. M., & Waage, P. (1864). Studies concerning affinity.
*Forhandlinger: Videnskabs-Selskabet i Christiania*. (Law of mass action.)
- Kacser, H., & Burns, J. A. (1973). The control of flux.
*Symp. Soc. Exp. Biol.*27, 65–104. (Metabolic Control Analysis; flux-control summation theorem.)
- Palsson, B. Ø. (2015). *Systems Biology: Constraint-based Reconstruction and Analysis*. Cambridge University Press. DOI:[10.1017/CBO9781139854610](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139854610)

---

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^2.0/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display``#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {max})", max = i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From``#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()``#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()``Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace``Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()``provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and`Display``#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

---

# yatrosci_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-core/^0.1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-core)SciRS Core

Core traits, types, and error handling for the SciRS scientific computing ecosystem.

This crate provides the foundational abstractions used throughout SciRS:

- `Scalar`trait for numeric types
- `Float`trait for floating-point operations
- Complex number utilities
- Error types and result aliases
- Precision control

[§](https://docs.rs#canonical-references)Canonical References

The `Float` and `Scalar` traits expose IEEE 754-2019 standard operations
(epsilon, infinity, NaN, fused multiply-add) with no deviation from the standard.
All implementations delegate to the `num-traits` crate which in turn delegates
to the Rust standard library’s IEEE 754-compliant primitives.

- IEEE (2019). *IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic*(IEEE 754-2019). DOI:[10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229](https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229)
- Higham, N.J. (2002). *Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms*(2nd ed.), §2.2 (Floating-point arithmetic model), pp. 36–50. SIAM. DOI:[10.1137/1.9780898718027](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027)

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yatrosci_core::{Scalar, Float, Complex64};
fn compute<T: Float>(x: T) -> T {
    x.sin() + x.cos()
}
```

# approx - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/approx/^0.5/

## Expand description

A crate that provides facilities for testing the approximate equality of floating-point based types, using either relative difference, or units in the last place (ULPs) comparisons.

You can also use the `*_{eq, ne}!` and `assert_*_{eq, ne}!` macros to test for equality using a
more positional style:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate approx;
use std::f64;
abs_diff_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
abs_diff_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_relative = 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON, max_relative = 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_relative = 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_ulps = 4);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON, max_ulps = 4);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_ulps = 4, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-approximate-equality-for-custom-types)Implementing approximate equality for custom types

The `*Eq` traits allow approximate equalities to be implemented on types, based on the
fundamental floating point implementations.

For example, we might want to be able to do approximate assertions on a complex number type:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate approx;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Complex<T> {
    x: T,
    i: T,
}
let x = Complex { x: 1.2, i: 2.3 };
assert_relative_eq!(x, x);
assert_ulps_eq!(x, x, max_ulps = 4);
```
To do this we can implement [ AbsDiffEq](https://docs.rs/trait.AbsDiffEq.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/trait.RelativeEq.html)

`RelativeEq`[generically in terms of a type parameter that also implements](https://docs.rs/trait.UlpsEq.html)

`UlpsEq``AbsDiffEq`, `RelativeEq` and `UlpsEq` respectively.
This means that we can make comparisons for either `Complex<f32>` or `Complex<f64>`:```
impl<T: AbsDiffEq> AbsDiffEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    type Epsilon = T::Epsilon;
    fn default_epsilon() -> T::Epsilon {
        T::default_epsilon()
    }
    fn abs_diff_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon) -> bool {
        T::abs_diff_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon) &&
        T::abs_diff_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon)
    }
}
impl<T: RelativeEq> RelativeEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    fn default_max_relative() -> T::Epsilon {
        T::default_max_relative()
    }
    fn relative_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon, max_relative: T::Epsilon) -> bool {
        T::relative_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon, max_relative) &&
        T::relative_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon, max_relative)
    }
}
impl<T: UlpsEq> UlpsEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    fn default_max_ulps() -> u32 {
        T::default_max_ulps()
    }
    fn ulps_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon, max_ulps: u32) -> bool {
        T::ulps_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon, max_ulps) &&
        T::ulps_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon, max_ulps)
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#references)References

Floating point is hard! Thanks goes to these links for helping to make things a *little*
easier to understand:

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [abs_](https://docs.rs/macro.abs_diff_eq.html)- diff_ - eq
- Approximate equality of using the absolute difference.
- [abs_](https://docs.rs/macro.abs_diff_ne.html)- diff_ - ne
- Approximate inequality of using the absolute difference.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_abs_diff_eq.html)- abs_ - diff_ - eq
- An assertion that delegates to `abs_diff_eq!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_abs_diff_ne.html)- abs_ - diff_ - ne
- An assertion that delegates to `abs_diff_ne!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_relative_eq.html)- relative_ - eq
- An assertion that delegates to `relative_eq!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_relative_ne.html)- relative_ - ne
- An assertion that delegates to `relative_ne!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ulps_eq.html)- ulps_ - eq
- An assertion that delegates to `ulps_eq!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ulps_ne.html)- ulps_ - ne
- An assertion that delegates to `ulps_ne!`
- [relative_](https://docs.rs/macro.relative_eq.html)- eq
- Approximate equality using both the absolute difference and relative based comparisons.
- [relative_](https://docs.rs/macro.relative_ne.html)- ne
- Approximate inequality using both the absolute difference and relative based comparisons.
- [ulps_eq](https://docs.rs/macro.ulps_eq.html)
- Approximate equality using both the absolute difference and ULPs (Units in Last Place).
- [ulps_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.ulps_ne.html)
- Approximate inequality using both the absolute difference and ULPs (Units in Last Place).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AbsDiff](https://docs.rs/struct.AbsDiff.html)
- The requisite parameters for testing for approximate equality using a absolute difference based comparison.
- [Relative](https://docs.rs/struct.Relative.html)
- The requisite parameters for testing for approximate equality using a relative based comparison.
- [Ulps](https://docs.rs/struct.Ulps.html)
- The requisite parameters for testing for approximate equality using an ULPs based comparison.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AbsDiff](https://docs.rs/trait.AbsDiffEq.html)- Eq
- Equality that is defined using the absolute difference of two numbers.
- [Relative](https://docs.rs/trait.RelativeEq.html)- Eq
- Equality comparisons between two numbers using both the absolute difference and relative based comparisons.
- [UlpsEq](https://docs.rs/trait.UlpsEq.html)
- Equality comparisons between two numbers using both the absolute difference and ULPs (Units in Last Place) based comparisons.

# yatrosci_bio_systems - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yatrosci-bio-systems/0.1.0/target-redirect/yatrosci_bio_systems/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-systems-biology-advanced)SciRS Systems Biology (Advanced)

Formal modeling of biological networks and systems. No simplified equations.

This crate provides:

- Mass-action kinetics (law of mass action, reaction order)
- Metabolic Control Analysis (MCA) (Elasticities, Control coefficients)
- Stoichiometric Modeling (Flux Balance Analysis foundations)
- Gene Regulatory Networks (Hill kinetics, cooperativity, Hill plot)

[§](https://docs.rs#references)References

- Hill, A. V. (1910). The possible effects of the aggregation of the
molecules of haemoglobin on its dissociation curves.
*J. Physiol.*40, iv–vii.
- Guldberg, C. M., & Waage, P. (1864). Studies concerning affinity.
*Forhandlinger: Videnskabs-Selskabet i Christiania*. (Law of mass action.)
- Kacser, H., & Burns, J. A. (1973). The control of flux.
*Symp. Soc. Exp. Biol.*27, 65–104. (Metabolic Control Analysis; flux-control summation theorem.)
- Palsson, B. Ø. (2015). *Systems Biology: Constraint-based Reconstruction and Analysis*. Cambridge University Press. DOI:[10.1017/CBO9781139854610](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139854610)

[29](https://docs.rs#29)use yatrosci_core::Float;
[30](https://docs.rs#30)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)/// Mass-action kinetics (law of mass action).
[32](https://docs.rs#32)pub mod mass_action {
[33](https://docs.rs#33)    use super::*;
[34](https://docs.rs#34)
[35](https://docs.rs#35)    /// Reaction rate by the law of mass action:
[36](https://docs.rs#36)    /// `v = k · ∏ᵢ [Xᵢ]^{aᵢ}`, with kinetic orders `orders` for each species.
[37](https://docs.rs#37)    ///
[38](https://docs.rs#38)    /// REF: Guldberg & Waage (1864).
[39](https://docs.rs#39)    pub fn reaction_rate<T: Float>(k: T, concentrations: &[T], orders: &[T]) -> T {
[40](https://docs.rs#40)        assert_eq!(
[41](https://docs.rs#41)            concentrations.len(),
[42](https://docs.rs#42)            orders.len(),
[43](https://docs.rs#43)            "concentration and order slices must have equal length"
[44](https://docs.rs#44)        );
[45](https://docs.rs#45)        concentrations
[46](https://docs.rs#46)            .iter()
[47](https://docs.rs#47)            .zip(orders.iter())
[48](https://docs.rs#48)            .fold(k, |acc, (&c, &a)| acc * c.powf(a))
[49](https://docs.rs#49)    }
[50](https://docs.rs#50)}
[51](https://docs.rs#51)
[52](https://docs.rs#52)/// Stoichiometric and Flux Analysis
[53](https://docs.rs#53)pub mod metabolism {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)    use super::*;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)
[56](https://docs.rs#56)    /// Steady-state condition: S * v = 0
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    /// where S is the Stoichiometric Matrix and v is the flux vector
[58](https://docs.rs#58)    pub struct Stoichiometry<T: Float> {
[59](https://docs.rs#59)        /// Matrix rows: metabolites, columns: reactions
[60](https://docs.rs#60)        pub matrix: Vec<Vec<T>>,
[61](https://docs.rs#61)    }
[62](https://docs.rs#62)
[63](https://docs.rs#63)    /// Mass balance check for a reaction vector v
[64](https://docs.rs#64)    pub fn is_steady_state<T: Float>(s: &Stoichiometry<T>, v: &[T], tolerance: T) -> bool {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)        for row in &s.matrix {
[66](https://docs.rs#66)            let sum = row
[67](https://docs.rs#67)                .iter()
[68](https://docs.rs#68)                .zip(v.iter())
[69](https://docs.rs#69)                .map(|(&si, &vi)| si * vi)
[70](https://docs.rs#70)                .fold(<T as yatrosci_core::Zero>::zero(), |acc, x| acc + x);
[71](https://docs.rs#71)            if yatrosci_core::NumFloat::abs(sum) > tolerance {
[72](https://docs.rs#72)                return false;
[73](https://docs.rs#73)            }
[74](https://docs.rs#74)        }
[75](https://docs.rs#75)        true
[76](https://docs.rs#76)    }
[77](https://docs.rs#77)}
[78](https://docs.rs#78)
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// Regulatory Kinetics
[80](https://docs.rs#80)pub mod regulation {
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    use super::*;
[82](https://docs.rs#82)
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    /// Hill Equation for cooperative binding: `v = Vmax·[S]^n / (Km^n + [S]^n)`.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)    ///
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    /// `n` is the Hill coefficient (cooperativity): `n=1` is hyperbolic
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    /// (non-cooperative) Michaelis-Menten, `n>1` positive cooperativity.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    /// REF: Hill (1910).
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    pub fn hill_kinetics<T: Float>(v_max: T, s: T, km: T, n: T) -> T {
[89](https://docs.rs#89)        let sn = s.powf(n);
[90](https://docs.rs#90)        let kmn = km.powf(n);
[91](https://docs.rs#91)        v_max * sn / (kmn + sn)
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    }
[93](https://docs.rs#93)
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    /// Fractional occupancy `θ = [S]^n / (Km^n + [S]^n)` (= v/Vmax).
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    pub fn hill_occupancy<T: Float>(s: T, km: T, n: T) -> T {
[96](https://docs.rs#96)        let sn = s.powf(n);
[97](https://docs.rs#97)        let kmn = km.powf(n);
[98](https://docs.rs#98)        sn / (kmn + sn)
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    }
[100](https://docs.rs#100)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    /// Hill-plot ordinate `ln[θ/(1−θ)]`, whose slope versus `ln[S]` is the
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    /// Hill coefficient `n` (the operational definition of cooperativity).
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    pub fn hill_plot_value<T: Float>(occupancy: T) -> T {
[104](https://docs.rs#104)        let one = <T as yatrosci_core::One>::one();
[105](https://docs.rs#105)        (occupancy / (one - occupancy)).ln()
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    }
[107](https://docs.rs#107)}
[108](https://docs.rs#108)
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// Sensitivity and Control
[110](https://docs.rs#110)pub mod control {
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    use super::*;
[112](https://docs.rs#112)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    /// Elasticity Coefficient: ε_v_S = (∂v/∂S) * (S/v)
[114](https://docs.rs#114)    pub fn elasticity<T: Float>(dv_ds: T, s: T, v: T) -> T {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)        dv_ds * (s / v)
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    }
[117](https://docs.rs#117)}
[118](https://docs.rs#118)
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// Error type for systems biology

[121](https://docs.rs#121)pub enum BioSystemsError {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// Infeasible flux distribution
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    #[error("Infeasible metabolic flux")]
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    InfeasibleFlux,
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// Numerical instability
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    #[error("Numerical error: {0}")]
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    Numerical(String),
[128](https://docs.rs#128)}
[129](https://docs.rs#129)
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// Result type
[131](https://docs.rs#131)pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, BioSystemsError>;
[132](https://docs.rs#132)
[133](https://docs.rs#133)#[cfg(test)]
[134](https://docs.rs#134)mod tests {
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    use super::*;
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[137](https://docs.rs#137)
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    #[test]
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    fn stoichiometric_steady_state_checks_s_times_flux_zero() {
[140](https://docs.rs#140)        let s = metabolism::Stoichiometry {
[141](https://docs.rs#141)            matrix: vec![vec![-1.0_f64, 1.0], vec![1.0, -1.0]],
[142](https://docs.rs#142)        };
[143](https://docs.rs#143)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        assert!(metabolism::is_steady_state(&s, &[2.0, 2.0], 1e-12));
[145](https://docs.rs#145)        assert!(!metabolism::is_steady_state(&s, &[2.0, 1.0], 1e-12));
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    }
[147](https://docs.rs#147)
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    #[test]
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    fn hill_kinetics_reaches_half_vmax_at_substrate_equal_km() {
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        // INVARIANT: v = Vmax/2 at [S]=Km for ANY Hill coefficient n.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        for n in [1.0_f64, 2.0, 4.0, 0.5] {
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            assert_relative_eq!(
[153](https://docs.rs#153)                regulation::hill_kinetics(10.0_f64, 2.0, 2.0, n),
[154](https://docs.rs#154)                5.0,
[155](https://docs.rs#155)                epsilon = 1e-13
[156](https://docs.rs#156)            );
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        }
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    }
[159](https://docs.rs#159)
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    #[test]
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    fn hill_with_unit_coefficient_reduces_to_michaelis_menten() {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)        // INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK: with n=1 the Hill equation must equal the
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        // Michaelis-Menten hyperbola Vmax·S/(Km+S) (computed independently).
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        let v_max = 7.0_f64;
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        let km = 3.0;
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        for &s in &[0.5_f64, 3.0, 10.0, 50.0] {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            let hill = regulation::hill_kinetics(v_max, s, km, 1.0);
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            let mm = v_max * s / (km + s);
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            assert_relative_eq!(hill, mm, epsilon = 1e-13);
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    }
[172](https://docs.rs#172)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    #[test]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    fn hill_plot_slope_equals_the_hill_coefficient() {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        // INVARIANT (operational definition of cooperativity): the slope of the
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        // Hill plot ln[θ/(1−θ)] vs ln[S] is exactly n, for any n.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)        let km = 2.0_f64;
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        for n in [1.0_f64, 2.5, 4.0] {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            let s1 = 1.3_f64;
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            let s2 = 3.1_f64;
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            let y1 = regulation::hill_plot_value(regulation::hill_occupancy(s1, km, n));
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            let y2 = regulation::hill_plot_value(regulation::hill_occupancy(s2, km, n));
[183](https://docs.rs#183)            let slope = (y2 - y1) / (s2.ln() - s1.ln());
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            assert_relative_eq!(slope, n, epsilon = 1e-12);
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        }
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    #[test]
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    fn mass_action_rate_scales_with_reaction_order() {
[190](https://docs.rs#190)        // INVARIANT: an elementary reaction of order a in a species scales as
[191](https://docs.rs#191)        // c^a. Doubling [A] in a first-order step doubles v; in a second-order
[192](https://docs.rs#192)        // (A+A) step it quadruples v. Independent of the rate constant.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        let k = 0.7_f64;
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        let v1 = mass_action::reaction_rate(k, &[1.0], &[1.0]);
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        let v1d = mass_action::reaction_rate(k, &[2.0], &[1.0]);
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        assert_relative_eq!(v1d / v1, 2.0, epsilon = 1e-13);
[197](https://docs.rs#197)
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        let v2 = mass_action::reaction_rate(k, &[1.0], &[2.0]);
[199](https://docs.rs#199)        let v2d = mass_action::reaction_rate(k, &[2.0], &[2.0]);
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        assert_relative_eq!(v2d / v2, 4.0, epsilon = 1e-13);
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    }
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    #[test]
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    fn mass_action_bimolecular_is_product_of_concentrations() {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        // INVARIANT: for A+B→C, v = k[A][B]; the rate at fixed product [A][B]
[206](https://docs.rs#206)        // is invariant under exchanging the concentrations.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        let k = 1.5_f64;
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        let v = mass_action::reaction_rate(k, &[2.0, 3.0], &[1.0, 1.0]);
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        assert_relative_eq!(v, k * 2.0 * 3.0, epsilon = 1e-13);
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        let v_swap = mass_action::reaction_rate(k, &[3.0, 2.0], &[1.0, 1.0]);
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        assert_relative_eq!(v, v_swap, epsilon = 1e-13);
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    #[test]
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    fn elasticity_of_power_law_rate_equals_kinetic_order() {
[216](https://docs.rs#216)        // INDEPENDENT INVARIANT: a power-law rate v=k·S^n has elasticity
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        // ε = (∂v/∂S)(S/v) = n exactly — its kinetic order. We feed the
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        // analytic derivative of an independent power law and recover n.
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        let k = 2.3_f64;
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        let s = 4.0_f64;
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        for n in [1.0_f64, 2.0, 0.5, 3.0] {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)            let v = k * s.powf(n);
[223](https://docs.rs#223)            let dv_ds = k * n * s.powf(n - 1.0);
[224](https://docs.rs#224)            assert_relative_eq!(control::elasticity(dv_ds, s, v), n, epsilon = 1e-12);
[225](https://docs.rs#225)        }
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    }
[227](https://docs.rs#227)}
